summary: Weekly POC sync focused on cost/unit economics. Reviewed recent benchmark runs showing tokens/sec and tokens/$ under different batching and caching configs. Discussed tradeoffs between latency and unit cost, caching hit-rate impact, and next steps to run a large-scale batch test and finalize pilot criteria.
topics: caching savings and prefix/KV cache hit rates
dedicated vs hosted routing and fallback policies
pilot success criteria and next steps
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: OK hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll kick off quick — this is our weekly POC sync, focus today on cost per unit economics, tokens per second and tokens per dollar. we have the benchmark outputs from last night.
[00:12] Samir: cool, yeah i'm interested in the caching numbers, last time the hit rate looked lower than we expected.
[00:18] Priya: hi all, priya from redwood runtime. i pulled the runs into the sheet, there's a couple of variants — no-cache baseline, prefix-cache enabled, and then batching at 8/16/32. i put notes in the spreadsheet: cost_breakdown_v3.xlsx in the shared drive.
[00:34] Lena: can you remind us what your units are for tokens/$ again? last month's sheet mixed units a bit so we want to align.
[00:40] Jordan: yes — tokens per dollar is computed as total tokens served divided by infra cost for the run; for hosted it's our list rate minus discounts, for dedicated we used equivalent hourly instance cost amortized. Priya, correct me if i'm off.
[00:51] Priya: that's right, we normalized to USD and included GPU amortization and swap overhead. it's a rough econ but useful for comparisons.
[00:58] Marcus: and latency numbers are p50/p95 right? because we care about tail for UX.
[01:03] Priya: we captured p50, p95, and median was close to p50. tail gets worse as batch size increases, unsurprisingly.
[01:11] Samir: OK, show us the numbers.
[01:13] Priya: sure — readout from last night's 4-hour run: baseline (no cache, batch=1) tokens/sec ~ 120 tps, tokens/$ ~ 480k tokens per dollar; with prefix cache enabled (assume 30% hit-rate observed) tokens/sec jumps to ~180 tps and tokens/$ to ~720k. with batching 16 and cache, tokens/sec ~600 tps but tokens/$ increases to ~2M, however p95 latency moved from 180ms to 820ms.
[01:42] Samir: hmm that 30% hit-rate assumption is optimistic for our traffic — in prod we have many unique prefixes, i'd estimate closer to 10-12%.
[01:50] Priya: noted — we do have a run where we simulated lower hit-rate, that one showed ~220 tps with 12% cache hit and tokens/$ ~880k. numbers are in the sheet.
[02:02] Lena: how are you measuring cache? is that KV cache or a prefix response cache? our app uses long conversations so KV reuse is the main expected win.
[02:11] Priya: good question — both can help; the run used KV cache for model key-value cache plus a small prefix cache for repeated static prompts. KV cache helps with long convo continuation; prefix cache helps when users repeat similar queries. we annotated which tests used which.
[02:23] Marcus: curious about memory overhead. when you enable KV cache, what's the per-session memory? we've seen memory pressure on our infra.
[02:29] Priya: per-session KV cache is proportional to seq length and kv entries; on our test model a 2k token context had about 50-80MB per active session when fully cached. we can configure eviction TTLs to manage memory; you can also use shared cache nodes to reduce per-instance overhead.
[02:45] Samir: so that affects cost because memory constraints limit batching and concurrency. is that included in the tokens/$ calc?
[02:51] Jordan: yes, we included memory footprint as part of the effective throughput; in dedicated scenarios if you need larger RAM GPUs that changes the hourly amortization.
[02:59] Lena: another variable is quantization — do you have runs with int8 vs float16? that changes perf a lot.
[03:05] Priya: we ran int8 quantized model on the latest kernel; int8 improved tokens/sec by ~1.6x vs fp16 and reduced memory too, but some quality variance on edge prompts — we flagged a couple failing eval cases.
[03:18] Samir: hmm quality tradeoff may not be acceptable for our compliance prompts. we need to see eval diffs.
[03:22] Priya: agreed — i'll attach the eval diff and the failing prompt examples.
[03:26] Marcus: what's the expected cost delta between hosted and dedicated for our projected QPS?
[03:30] Jordan: short answer — dedicated straight-line cost per token is about 30-40% lower at your targeted sustained QPS (60-80 rps generating ~400-600k tokens/hour), but that assumes you can fill reserved capacity. if you have big burstiness, the cost advantage shrinks unless you combine reserved with burst.
[03:47] Samir: we do have significant diurnal peaks — 3x peak over baseline, so burst capacity matters.
[03:51] Jordan: exactly. Redwood Dedicated supports burst pools and can be configured for autoscale; we modeled a hybrid where reserved handles baseline and hosted covers peaks; the blended tokens/$ was in the sheet — roughly 20% better than pure hosted for your profile.
[04:04] Priya: also there's routing policy — you can route latency-sensitive routes to lower-batch, low-latency instances and bulk/background to high-batch nodes. that preserves UX while keeping costs down.
[04:14] Lena: what's the overhead of routing complexity? does it add observability burden?
[04:18] Jordan: our console exposes per-route cost and latency breakdowns; route rules are simple JSON configs. there is some initial operational setup but we provide templates and we'll help onboard.
[04:28] Samir: one risk is cold-starts and model variants — how does fallback behave if a dedicated pool is saturated?
[04:34] Priya: automatic fallback to hosted compatible model variant is available; we also support canary and A/B rollout so you can test capacity gradually. fallback adds a small latency delta but keeps service up.
[04:44] Marcus: about the token accounting — our analytics team wants per-user cost attribution, can we tag tokens to customers/orders?
[04:50] Jordan: yes, you can instrument requests with metadata and our billing/export provides per-route and tag-level token breakdowns.
[04:58] Samir: ok back to the bench — what would be the recommended next test to close the delta on cache hit assumptions? we need a worst-case and a typical-case.
[05:05] Priya: recommendation: run two 4-hour runs on staging, one simulating your prod prefix distribution (low cache reuse ~10%) and one with synthetic repeat sessions to show best-case (30%+). we will then estimate blended tokens/$ and provide guidance on batching knobs that keep p95 under your threshold.
[05:20] Lena: we can simulate that if you give the benchmark script and the exact flags.
[05:23] Priya: i'll share the script and the kernel flags — see runtime_flags.txt in the drive. also we have a parameter for batch latency cap which will let you pick a max p95.
[05:34] Jordan: action items: we'll update cost_breakdown_v3.xlsx with a sheet that shows blended scenarios. we'll include dedicated vs hosted vs hybrid. Jordan will send that by Friday.
[05:43] Marcus: what about security docs? legal asked for SOC2 and KMS integration notes.
[05:48] Jordan: i'll include SOC2 summary and KMS/HSM integration whitepaper in the follow-up email, plus the security pack link we shared earlier.
[05:56] Samir: good. also can we run one short test with batching 8 and TTL 30s cache only to check memory footprint impact? that helps our infra team.
[06:05] Priya: yes we can. we'll schedule a run and share logs.
[06:09] Lena: one last question — you mentioned prefetching common prefixes to improve hit-rate; is that a supported workflow?
[06:15] Priya: yes, we have a pre-warm API to seed prefix cache and a managed process for bulk prefetch. that helps with known hot prompts.
[06:23] Jordan: ok we're running low on time. recap: Jordan to send updated cost model and security docs; Priya to share benchmark script and runtime flags and run the batching+cache test with Lena; Quantaco to confirm ROI and pilot criteria; schedule follow-up for Oct 15 to review results.
[06:40] Samir: thanks everyone.
[06:42] Marcus: thanks.
[06:43] Jordan: thanks all, bye.
